title: The Effect of AI on the Radiologist Workforce: A Task-Based Analysis
author: Curtis P. Langlotz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Clinical teaming: AI accuracy may worsen joint decisions
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether AI accuracy worsens human–AI clinical decisions or endorse self-calibration and local clinician testing. It instead reframes the issue around task-level productivity and workforce demand, arguing that projected time savings need not produce near-term radiologist job losses and are conditional on imaging growth.
qs: We used published evidence to estimate the effect of each AI application on each radiology task using a 5-year time horizon.
Our model suggests that radiologist job loss due to AI is unlikely in the next 5 years.

st.t: Human-AI decisions: Self-knowledge conditions unrealized gains
st.an: The source does not evaluate whether self-knowledge, case uncertainty or model error condition human–AI decision gains. Instead, it constructively reframes the inquiry as a task- and modality-specific assessment of AI’s potential workforce effects, extending analysis beyond image interpretation to pre-, intra- and post-procedure work.
qs: Because the effect of AI tools varies across imaging modalities, we estimated the fraction of time radiologists spend on interpreting studies from each modality based on the number of studies performed each year in the US [[17](#R17)–[22](#R22)], the percentage of those studies interpreted by radiologists, and a work RVU adjustment commonly used by radiology practice to measure productivity [[23](#R23)].

The AI applications and their definitions are shown below, grouped by pre-procedure, intra-procedure, and post-procedure applications:  ### Pre-procedure applications of AI to radiology  -  Order entry decision support for radiology test selection.** A decision is made whether a test is appropriate based on the patient’s clinical history and current symptoms.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source’s task-level methodology is compatible with the cluster’s emphasis on analysing workflow reconfiguration rather than treating an occupation as uniformly automatable. However, it concerns radiology, relies partly on author judgment, and the supplied material contains no findings on workforce displacement, productivity, verification, user competence or apprenticeship risks. It therefore does not establish a substantive position on the legal-workflow proposition.
qs: We used published evidence to estimate the effect of each AI application on each radiology task using a 5-year time horizon.
When published evidence was unavailable, we used our own judgment.

st.t: Clinical support: Practitioner gains may not help patients
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified framing: its bibliography identifies varied clinical decision-support outcomes, including one explicitly ineffective intervention, while providing insufficient evidence for broader claims about patient benefits or radiologist workforce effects. Because the supplied material is only references, it reinforces the need to distinguish intervention-specific findings from general conclusions.
qs: Effects of computerized clinical decision support systems on practitioner performance and patient outcomes: a systematic review: A systematic review.

st.t: Radiology assistance: Accuracy, teamwork and replacement diverge
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task-versus-job distinction by predicting that AI will raise productivity and absorb selected burdensome tasks without displacing radiologists. Its workforce conclusion is explicitly predictive and analogy-based, not evidence that non-displacement has already occurred, consistent with the cluster’s qualification.
qs: These results suggest that the effect of AI will be similar to prior waves of innovation in radiology, such as picture archiving and communication systems, which substantially improved productivity but did not displace radiologists.

Overall, these changes may improve the quality of life of radiologists by flattening the growth in their workload and by performing tasks that radiologists consider less interesting, such as lesion measurement and “needle-in-a-haystack” tasks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core task-redesign proposition through a task-based radiology model: AI’s effects vary by activity, may substantially reduce time on selected tasks, and are more likely to shift workload than eliminate the profession. Its employment conclusion is a qualified forecast, however, resting partly on judgment-based assumptions and unmodeled demand growth rather than observed displacement outcomes.
qs: This suggests AI may cause shifts among radiologist tasks, rather than a reduction in the need for radiologists.
Our conclusions about the overall effect on the radiology workforce depend on the future growth of imaging volumes, which was not explicitly modeled and may not continue.

kp.k: Task-based model predicts substantial reductions in required radiologist hours
kp.d: This 2025 preprint, not yet peer reviewed, projects a base-case 33% reduction in radiologist hours over five years, bounded by 14% and 49%. These are modeled effects based on published evidence and author judgment, not observed workforce reductions. Although the Results section also describes reduced need for radiologists, the employment conclusion depends separately on future imaging demand.
qs: The model projects a 33% reduction in hours worked by radiologists in 5 years, with a range of 14% to 49%.
When published evidence was unavailable, we used our own judgment.

kp.k: Task allocation combines small observational studies and modality weights
kp.d: The model averages task-time percentages from Dhanoa et al., observing 14 radiologists across three Canadian hospitals, and Schemmel et al., focusing on one neuroradiology fellow at an academic hospital. Performing and interpreting studies accounts for 66.7% of time and protocoling for 5.5%. Modality weights incorporate annual US study volumes, the share interpreted by radiologists and work RVU adjustments. Raising interpretation and reporting to 80% of working time produces a modeled 35% hours reduction.
qs: Dhanoa et al
We analyzed and categorized the tasks measured, then averaged the percentage of time spent in each category between the two studies.
The results showed a reduction in radiologist hours worked of 35%, indicating the model is relatively robust to modest changes in task distribution.

kp.k: Independent application effects are combined multiplicatively
kp.d: The model estimates base, lower and upper effects for application-task interactions, assuming independence and multiplying their effects rather than adding savings. It combines technologies currently available, such as detection and triage, with applications considered foreseeable within five years, such as automated report drafting.
qs: We assumed that the effects of each AI application on each task were independent.
For example, a 3% reduction in imaging volume due to order entry decision support is independent of the effect of report drafting, which would improve efficiency on the remaining 97% of orders.
Therefore, we multiplied the percentage effects of each AI application on each radiology task to arrive at the overall reduction in hours needed to accomplish that task.

kp.k: Report drafting is a principal projected productivity driver
kp.d: AI drafts reports for radiologist review and signature rather than eliminating human involvement. The author cites a 15% radiography productivity increase, anticipates greater gains for cross-sectional imaging and assumes a 20% base-case improvement, ranging from 10–30%. Drafting has a particularly strong modeled effect on CT and radiography because they account for substantial interpretation and reporting time.
qs: Large productivity gains could be achieved if reports are drafted automatically for review and signature.
Evidence in the literature cites a 15% productivity increase for radiography
We assumed a base case of 20% improvement in productivity, with a range of 10–30%.

kp.k: Study delegation removes selected cases from human interpretation
kp.d: The author reports studies identifying almost certainly normal cases suitable for no further human review: up to 50% of screening mammograms and 40% of outpatient radiographs. Combined with human interpretation of remaining cases, the cited systems reportedly achieve equivalent or improved accuracy. The model assumes interpretation-time effects of 50% for mammography, ranging from 30–60%, and 40% for radiography, ranging from 30–50%; delegation of 3% of other modalities, ranging from 1–5%, is explicitly speculative.
qs: When combined with human review of the remaining studies, these systems can provide equivalent or improved accuracy compared to a human-only system.
More evidence is needed, but these systems could have a large impact on radiologist workload in selected subspecialty areas.
Although speculative, we assumed a 3% delegation of all other modalities, with a range of 1–5%.

kp.k: Detection and triage offer limited expected workload savings
kp.d: Triage generally changes case order rather than the number requiring interpretation; the model assumes a 1% interpretation-time improvement, ranging from 0–5%. Detection may accelerate difficult searches but creates false-positive adjudication work. The author characterizes productivity evidence for chest radiographs as weak and absent for other study types, assuming 5% increased radiography productivity, ranging from 0–15%, and no base-case savings elsewhere, ranging from 5% savings to a 5% time increase. Disease classification receives a judgment-based 1% time saving, ranging from 0–5%, without published efficiency evidence.
qs: Otherwise, these tools have no appreciable effect on radiologist productivity because the same number of studies must be interpreted in a different order.

Detection systems may increase efficiency of “needle-in-a-haystack” tasks, such as detecting lung nodules, but may simultaneously decrease radiologists’ productivity by adding the need to adjudicate false positive detections.
There is no published evidence on the effect of diagnostic decision support on radiologist efficiency.

kp.k: Pre-procedure automation has uneven evidentiary support
kp.d: Order-entry decision support has mixed evidence, and newer machine-learning systems lack assessments of order-volume effects; the model assumes a 3% reduction in advanced imaging orders, ranging from 0–6%. Medical-history summarization lacks published radiologist productivity data but is assigned a 2% interpretation-time reduction, ranging from 0–4%, and 30% less communication with technologists and referrers, ranging from 10–50%. Protocol automation has more concrete supporting evidence: 69% of studies automatically protocoled at 95% accuracy informs an assumed 60% protocoling-time reduction, ranging from 30–70%.
qs: Despite past federally mandated implementation of these tools, imaging volume continued to increase.
There is no published data on how these systems affect radiologist productivity.
Recent work shows that 69% of studies could be protocoled automatically with 95% accuracy

kp.k: Additional findings and image-quality changes can increase work
kp.d: Opportunistic screening extracts findings radiologists ordinarily do not report, creating validation and reporting obligations. The model assumes a 2% workload increase, ranging from 0–5%, for CT and radiography. AI reconstruction can make acquisition more efficient without improving interpretation productivity: its base-case effect is zero, ranging from a 1% interpretation-time reduction to a 5% increase because image quality may be lower.
qs: These systems may decrease productivity because radiologists must validate and report the additional findings.
We assumed a base case increase in work by 2%, with a range of 0–5%.
Lower image quality may decrease productivity.

kp.k: Communication savings remain assumptions rather than measured productivity effects
kp.d: The author assumes AI support for urgent or unexpected findings reduces time communicating with referring clinicians by 30%, ranging from 20–50%, despite no published productivity evidence. Report-explanation systems are assigned a 30% reduction in patient communication needs, ranging from 10–50%, also without published productivity evidence. Such systems may improve understanding or care, but those benefits are distinct from demonstrated time savings.
qs: There is little work on AI-based solutions
There is no published evidence on the effect of these communication systems on radiologist productivity.
Future work may show these systems reduce patient calls or messages.

kp.k: Continued imaging growth underpins the no-job-loss prediction
kp.d: The author predicts radiologist job loss is unlikely over the next five years because rising imaging volumes and relatively static radiologist supply should offset productivity gains. The discussion cites near doubling of cross-sectional study volume over the preceding decade and anticipates continued demand growth, potentially changing task composition and slowing workload growth rather than reducing employment. Crucially, future volume growth is not explicitly modeled and may not persist.
qs: Our model suggests that radiologist job loss due to AI is unlikely in the next 5 years.
The productivity gains from AI are likely to be offset by continued growth in imaging volumes, causing continued growth in the need for radiologists, albeit at a slower rate.
Our conclusions about the overall effect on the radiology workforce depend on the future growth of imaging volumes, which was not explicitly modeled and may not continue.

kp.k: Adoption constraints make projected effects potentially upper-end estimates
kp.d: The author cautions that implementation will be phased, depend on organizational resources and returns on investment, and vary across institutions. Not all organizations will adopt every algorithm, and AI-only interpretation of normal studies may encounter substantial resistance. The model also excludes the productivity costs of new monitoring and oversight tasks.
qs: The projected workforce effects of AI likely represent the upper end of a range.
It is unlikely that all organizations will adopt all these algorithms.
Some changes, such as the delegation of normal studies to AI-only interpretation, may face significant resistance to adoption.
We did not explicitly consider the productivity effects of new AI governance tasks such as the monitoring and oversight of deployed AI algorithms.

kp.k: Evidence gaps and aggregation limit generalizability
kp.d: Many assumptions derive from the author's experience because reliable measurements are unavailable. Short time-and-motion studies favor academic practice; the model does not separately estimate modality subtypes such as screening versus diagnostic mammography, and groups procedural work with interpretation and reporting. Its US-centric modality distribution and reading practices limit transferability to countries with different practices, including double reading of mammograms.
qs: There are no reliable measurements of the effects of AI on many radiology tasks, so many of the model assumptions were estimated from the author’s experience and observations.
The published time and motion studies we used to estimate how radiologists spend their time were short in duration and were weighted towards academic practice.
Our analysis lumped procedural components of work with interpretation and reporting.
The analysis is U.S.-centric.

kp.k: Productivity gains may improve work quality without occupational displacement
kp.d: The author suggests AI could improve radiologists' quality of life by flattening workload growth and performing less interesting tasks, including lesion measurement and difficult searches. Given shortages in most areas, reduced volume or slower growth might be welcomed. The conclusion invokes prior radiology innovations, particularly picture archiving and communication systems, as an analogy for productivity growth without displacement; these are expectations and historical comparisons, not measured outcomes of the model.
qs: Because there is a shortage of radiologists in most areas, some decrease in volume (or decrease in growth rate) might be welcomed by radiologists.

These results suggest that the effect of AI will be similar to prior waves of innovation in radiology, such as picture archiving and communication systems, which substantially improved productivity but did not displace radiologists.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Langlotz predicts substantial reductions in radiologist task-hours, but not radiologist job losses, over five years.
pts.d: In this cross-domain source, Langlotz's task-based model projects a 33% base-case reduction in radiologist hours required, bounded by 14% and 49%. These are modeled productivity effects, not observed employment reductions. Although the Results section also describes a reduction in the 'need for radiologists', the Discussion and Conclusion distinguish task-hours from workforce demand: continued imaging-volume growth and relatively static radiologist supply are expected to offset productivity gains, leaving demand for radiologists growing more slowly rather than declining.

pts.k: Report drafting with human review and delegation without human interpretation are predicted to produce the largest workload savings.
pts.d: Langlotz distinguishes augmentation through automatically drafted reports reviewed and signed by radiologists from substitution through delegation of selected studies to AI-only interpretation. Table 1 models report drafting as a 20% reduction in interpretation time, with a 10–30% range; the prose describes this as a productivity improvement. Delegation is assumed to reduce mammography interpretation work by 50% (30–60%), radiography work by 40% (30–50%), and other modalities by 3% (1–5%), the latter explicitly speculative. CT, radiography and mammography account for the largest overall effects.

pts.k: Detection and triage are expected to have limited productivity effects, while some AI applications add work.
pts.d: Langlotz assumes a 1% interpretation-time saving from triage (0–5%) because reordering studies generally does not remove interpretations. Detection is assigned a 5% base-case productivity gain for radiography (0–15%), but no base-case time saving for other modalities, with outcomes ranging from 5% less to 5% more time. False-positive adjudication can offset detection savings. Opportunistic screening is assumed to increase CT and radiography interpretation work by 2% (0–5%) because additional findings require validation and reporting. Image reconstruction has no base-case productivity effect, with a range from 1% less interpretation time to 5% more.

pts.k: AI is also modeled as reducing protocol selection, information-search and communication work, and modestly reducing imaging orders.
pts.d: Langlotz assumes advanced-imaging orders decline 3% (0–6%) through order-entry decision support; history summarization reduces interpretation time 2% (0–4%) and communication with technologists and referrers 30% (10–50%); automated protocoling reduces protocoling time 60% (30–70%); disease classification saves 1% of interpretation time (0–5%); non-routine communication tools reduce referring-clinician communication time 30% (20–50%); and report explanations reduce patient-communication needs 30% (10–50%). These are application-specific modeling assumptions, not measured profession-wide reductions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The aggregate projection combines observational task measurements, published application studies and the author's judgment; it is not an observed workforce outcome.
pts.d: The supplied source is a 2025 medRxiv preprint identified as not yet peer reviewed. Task shares average two short observational studies: one observing 14 radiologists at three Canadian hospitals and one focusing on an academic neuroradiology fellow. Performing and interpreting studies accounts for 66.7% of baseline time. Modality weights use US study volumes, radiologist interpretation shares and work-RVU adjustments. Application effects are assumed independent and combined multiplicatively. Raising interpretation/reporting to 80% of working time yields a 35% modeled hours reduction. Langlotz acknowledges that many effects lack reliable measurements and are estimated from his experience; the reported bounds are model-assumption bounds, not presented as statistical confidence intervals.

pts.k: The source distinguishes published support for selected applications from unmeasured or speculative productivity effects.
pts.d: Langlotz cites studies supporting delegation of up to 50% of screening mammograms and 40% of outpatient radiographs, including retrospective analyses and a simulation study, while saying more evidence is needed. He reports published evidence of a 15% radiography productivity increase from drafting and extrapolates to a larger modeled effect across modalities. Automated protocoling is supported by a reported 69% automation rate at 95% accuracy. Detection productivity evidence for chest radiographs is described as weak. The source reports no published radiologist-productivity evidence for history summarization, diagnostic decision support, non-routine communication or report-explanation systems. The employment prediction invokes historical imaging growth and projected supply, but future imaging demand is not explicitly modeled.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The five-year projection depends on adoption and continued demand growth, and may overstate realized productivity effects.
pts.d: The model covers technologies available at publication and those considered foreseeable within five years, approximately through 2030. Langlotz says implementation will be phased, investment depends on organizational resources and returns, not every organization will adopt every algorithm, and AI-only interpretation may face resistance. Employment conclusions specifically depend on imaging-volume growth continuing. Other qualifications include academic-weighted task data, variation across practices and subspecialties, no separate modeling of modality subtypes, procedural work grouped with interpretation/reporting, and omission of new AI monitoring and oversight tasks.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects vary across radiology modalities, practice settings and countries; radiologists may experience slower workload growth and less routine work.
pts.d: The analysis primarily concerns US radiologists, with the largest modeled hours effects in CT, radiography and mammography. Practices without trainees may use report drafting in a trainee-like supporting role. Patients, referring clinicians and technologists are affected through report explanations and changed communication processes. Langlotz suggests radiologists may gain quality-of-life benefits from flatter workload growth and automation of less interesting tasks, particularly where shortages exist. He identifies students and trainees as stakeholders, but makes no separate quantified training or entry-level employment forecast. The source offers no direct prediction about legal services.
